edges.description: In pregnancy, maternal viremia can infect the placenta and fetus.
edges.target: Transplacental transmission and congenital rubella syndrome

nodes.description: Rubella virus is acquired by inhalation of respiratory droplets, replicating in nasopharyngeal mucosa and regional lymph nodes (producing the characteristic lymphadenopathy) before a viremia disseminates the virus.

evidence.snippet: Clinical disease often results in mild, self-limited illness characterised by fever, a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash, and lymphadenopathy.

nodes.description: Maternal viremia during early gestation infects the placenta and fetus. Rubella virus induces apoptosis and disrupts cell proliferation in fetal cells (the rubella capsid protein perturbs mitochondrial distribution via host protein p32), disrupting organogenesis during critical developmental windows and producing the cataract, cardiac, and cochlear defects of congenital rubella syndrome.
nodes.id: Transplacental transmission and congenital rubella syndrome

evidence.snippet: the fetus is most vulnerable to the rubella virus during the first trimester of pregnancy, due to the lack of immune defense in the developing fetus

evidence.reference_title: Interactions between rubella virus capsid and host protein p32 are important for virus replication.
evidence.snippet: capsid expression has been reported to cause apoptosis in certain cell types, suggesting that this protein may play a role in the cytopathic effect of the virus

evidence.reference_title: Interactions between rubella virus capsid and host protein p32 are important for virus replication.
evidence.snippet: The distribution and morphology of mitochondria are dramatically affected during infection with rubella virus (RV).

nodes.description: Systemic viremia seeds the skin, where an immune-mediated response produces the fine, transient maculopapular rash; rash onset coincides with the appearance of neutralizing antibody.
